# 6.11 Inflation and Real Returns: Key file (for the AI tutor only)

Do not reveal anything here before the learner has answered.

## Lesson facts relevant to the questions

- The learner has studied the Fisher equation and real rates (Lesson 1.3, "Intertemporal Choice" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/1-3-intertemporal-choice/), the CPI (Lesson 2.1, "Macroeconomic Data" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/2-1-macro-data/), business cycles and stock-bond correlation (Lesson 2.8, "Business Cycles and Asset Prices" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/2-8-business-cycle-asset-prices/), duration and immunization (Lesson 3.4, "Interest Rate Risk" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-4-interest-rate-risk/), TIPS and breakeven inflation (Lesson 3.6, "Credit Risk" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-6-credit-risk/), capital market assumptions (Lesson 4.11, "Capital Market Assumptions" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-11-capital-market-assumptions/), alternative assets (Lesson 5.5, "Alternative Assets" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/5-5-alternative-assets/), accounts and taxes (Lesson 6.5, "Accounts and Taxes (US)" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/6-5-accounts-taxes/), the household balance sheet and mortgages (Lesson 6.6, "The Household Balance Sheet and Insurance" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/6-6-household-balance-sheet/) and retirement planning (Lesson 6.9, "Retirement Planning" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/6-9-retirement-planning/). Percentages in percentage points.
- The lesson: money illusion; plan in today's purchasing power and real returns; Social Security adjusts for inflation, while most private pensions, ordinary annuities and fixed mortgage payments are fixed nominal amounts. Figure 1-1: real value of a fixed nominal 1,000 a year; slider inflation 0–8% (steps of 0.5, default 3); at 3%, about 744, 554, 412 after 10, 20, 30 years; at 5%, about 614, 377, 231.
- The lesson: cash and bills keep up in the short run but often earn near 0 real; nominal bonds suffer from unexpected inflation, more at longer maturities; TIPS held to maturity guarantee a real return; I bonds: a fixed rate plus an inflation rate reset every six months from the CPI, not traded, redeemable at accrued value, nominal value never falls, held at least 1 year, redeeming within 5 years forfeits the last 3 months of interest, at most 10,000 dollars a person a year, federal tax at redemption, state-tax exempt; November 2026–April 2027 fixed rate 1.40%, composite 5.51%. Stocks keep up in the long run, but unexpected inflation in the short run brings higher rates and lower valuations; commodities and real estate are somewhat positively related; fixed-rate liabilities favor borrowers. The lesson does not give the I bond composite rate formula (left to Exercises Question 3).
- The lesson: most retirement spending rises with prices, a real liability; a ladder of TIPS maturing one per year can match it; the same idea as immunization, with a real liability in place of a nominal one.
- The lesson: the CPI is the average price change of an urban consumer basket; households spend differently; retirees spend more on health care and housing, whose prices often rise faster; the BLS publishes the experimental CPI-E weighted for households 62 and over; Social Security adjusts by the CPI-W, 2.8% in 2026.

## Check question C1

A 65-year-old retiree has a pension of 3,000 dollars a month that does not adjust for inflation. Following the pattern in Figure 1-1, with 3% inflation, which statement is most accurate?

- (A) By 85, the pension buys only a little over half of what it does now ← Correct answer
- (B) The amount stays 3,000 dollars, so his standard of living is unchanged
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): Will 3,000 dollars buy as much in 20 years as today? Look at the readout for 20 years.
- (C) 3% inflation cuts only 3% a year, so after 20 years purchasing power falls by about 60%, leaving 40%
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): Inflation compounds, and each year removes about 3% of the remaining purchasing power. Roughly what is $\frac{1}{1.03^{20}}$?

**Reference answer**

(A). $\frac{1}{1.03^{20}} \approx 0.554$: about 55% of the purchasing power is left after 20 years and about 41% after 30. An income fixed in nominal terms loses much of its value over a long retirement; plans should be made in real terms and supplemented with Social Security, TIPS, stocks or other assets that keep up with inflation.

## Check question C2

A household has a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage and also holds many long-term nominal Treasuries. If inflation rises sharply and unexpectedly over the next few years, the household's real net worth:

- (A) Suffers on the asset side from the bonds, but gains on the liability side as the mortgage's real burden falls; the two partly offset ← Correct answer
- (B) Can only suffer, because the bonds lose real value
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): The mortgage is a fixed nominal amount. When inflation rises, what happens to the real value of this debt?
- (C) Is unaffected, because the house's price rises with inflation
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): House prices may keep up with inflation, but the question is about the bonds and the mortgage. How is each affected?

**Reference answer**

(A). Unexpected inflation lowers the real value of long nominal bonds (rates rise, prices fall) and also lowers the real burden of a fixed-rate mortgage: future payments are made in cheaper dollars. Inflation risk should be judged on the whole household balance sheet (Lesson 6.6, "The Household Balance Sheet and Insurance" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/6-6-household-balance-sheet/): holding nominal bonds while owing a fixed-rate mortgage, the two exposures partly offset; the net exposure depends on their sizes and durations (Exercises Question 4).

## Check question C3

In November 2026 the I bond's composite rate is 5.51%, and the 5-year TIPS real yield is about 2.31%. So over 5 years, the I bond's real return is clearly higher than TIPS'.

Correct answer: False

Hint (give it after a wrong answer, without the verdict): What two parts make up the I bond's composite rate? Which part is the real return after inflation? Which number should be compared with the TIPS real yield?

**Reference answer**

False. 5.51% is a nominal rate that includes the current inflation part of about 4.08%; the I bond's real return is set mainly by its fixed rate of 1.40%. Against the TIPS real yield of 2.31%, the I bond's real return is about 0.9 percentage points lower. The I bond's advantages lie elsewhere: its nominal value never falls, interest can be taxed only at redemption, and it is state-tax exempt; but it has purchase limits and holding restrictions. (TIPS are also state-tax exempt, but their inflation adjustments are taxed federally every year, Lesson 3.6, "Credit Risk" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-6-credit-risk/.)

## Check question C4

A retiree wants a fixed amount of spending money in today's prices each year for the next 10 years. Compared with holding an intermediate nominal bond fund, a ladder of TIPS maturing one per year is better because:

- (A) Each year's maturing amount adjusts for inflation and arrives when needed, matching real spending in both amount and timing, unaffected by changes in rates and inflation ← Correct answer
- (B) TIPS always have higher expected returns than nominal bonds
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): Their expected returns depend on actual versus breakeven inflation (Lesson 3.6, "Credit Risk" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-6-credit-risk/). Is the ladder's advantage a higher return or lower risk?
- (C) A bond fund cannot be sold
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): A bond fund can be sold at any time. The issue is what it fetches when sold, and whether that covers the year's real spending.

**Reference answer**

(A). A TIPS ladder matches a real liability with real assets: each TIPS held to maturity pays a certain real amount just when that year's spending is due, the same idea as immunization (Lesson 3.4, "Interest Rate Risk" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-4-interest-rate-risk/). A nominal bond fund has no maturity date; what it fetches depends on rates at the time of sale, and its nominal value does not adjust for inflation: if inflation rises unexpectedly, rising rates cut the fund's price just as spending goes up. The ladder's advantage is lower risk, not necessarily a higher return.

## Check question C5

If the CPI rose 2.8% over a year, then every retiree's cost of living rose by about 2.8% that year.

Correct answer: False

Hint (give it after a wrong answer, without the verdict): The CPI is the average price of which basket? Is a retiree's spending the same as that basket?

**Reference answer**

False. The CPI tracks the price of an average urban consumer's basket; a person's inflation rate depends on their own spending. Retirees spend larger shares on health care and housing, whose prices often rise faster than average; people who have paid off their homes are not hit by rent increases; people who drive a lot are hit more by fuel prices. So retirement plans may assume spending grows a bit faster than the CPI, especially health spending.

## Exercises Question 1 (id: Q1)

A 35-year-old investor sees an online calculator saying: "To retire at 65, you need 2 million dollars." The calculator assumes 3% inflation and a 7% nominal return.
(a) What is 2 million dollars in 30 years worth in today's purchasing power (thousand dollars)? What real return corresponds to the 7% nominal return?
(b) He says: "At 4% a year, 2 million dollars gives 80,000 dollars a year, enough for my current 70,000 dollars a year of spending." Evaluate this statement, and say how to avoid this kind of mistake.

**Reference answer**

(a) $\frac{2000}{1.03^{30}} \approx 824$ (thousand dollars). The real return is $\frac{1.07}{1.03} - 1 \approx 3.88\%$ (Lesson 1.3, "Intertemporal Choice" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/1-3-intertemporal-choice/).
(b) The statement is wrong. He treated a nominal amount 30 years away as today's purchasing power. In today's prices 2 million dollars is worth only about 824,000, which at 4% gives about 33,000 a year in today's purchasing power, far below 70,000. Sustaining 70,000 a year in today's money at 4% takes about 1.75 million in today's purchasing power, about $1750 \times 1.03^{30} \approx 4248$ thousand nominal in 30 years. To avoid this: state every goal in today's purchasing power, compute with the real return (about 3.88%), and read results in today's purchasing power; or use nominal amounts throughout, consistently on both sides.

**Grading points**

- (a) OK: about 824 (thousand dollars), real return about 3.88%.
- (b) OK: says nominal and real were mixed, and only about 33,000 a year is available in today's money; gives the method of using real (or nominal) amounts consistently. Agreeing it is enough needs revision.

Numeric answers: pv = 824, real = 3.88

**Common errors**

- Mixing nominal target amounts with real returns, or taking a future nominal amount as today's purchasing power.

## Exercises Question 2 (id: Q2)

A 65-year-old retiree wants 40,000 dollars (in today's purchasing power) at the end of each of the next 10 years. TIPS at all maturities yield 1.8% real, and nominal Treasuries at all maturities yield 4.2%.
(a) How much does a TIPS ladder providing this spending cost today (thousand dollars)? How much does a nominal Treasury ladder paying a fixed 40,000 nominal dollars a year cost? With 3% inflation, how much would nominal Treasuries cost to pay the inflation-adjusted amounts $40 \times 1.03^t$?
(b) He says: "The nominal ladder costs only 320,000 dollars and TIPS 360,000, so obviously choose nominal." Evaluate this statement.

**Reference answer**

(a) TIPS: $40 \times \frac{1 - 1.018^{-10}}{0.018} \approx 363.09$ (thousand dollars). Fixed nominal: $40 \times \frac{1 - 1.042^{-10}}{0.042} \approx 321.23$. Inflation-adjusted amounts at 3%: $\sum_{t=1}^{10} \frac{40 \times 1.03^t}{1.042^t} \approx 375.52$.
(b) The statement is wrong; the two do not buy the same thing. The 321 nominal ladder pays 40,000 nominal dollars a year, whose purchasing power falls year by year: at 3% inflation, 40,000 in year 10 is worth only about 29,800 today. Providing the same real amounts as TIPS with nominal bonds would cost about 375.52 at 3% inflation, more than TIPS; the nominal ladder is cheaper only if inflation turns out below the breakeven rate (about $\frac{1.042}{1.018} - 1 \approx 2.36\%$, Lesson 3.6, "Credit Risk" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-6-credit-risk/). More important, inflation is uncertain: the TIPS ladder locks in real spending, while the nominal ladder leaves him bearing inflation risk, and retirees are the people least able to bear it.

**Grading points**

- (a) OK: about 363.09, 321.23 and 375.52 (thousand dollars).
- (b) OK: says the two provide different cash flows (nominal versus real); uses breakeven inflation to show which is cheaper depends on actual inflation; notes TIPS remove inflation risk. Agreeing to choose nominal needs revision.

Numeric answers: tips = 363.09, fixed = 321.23, nom3 = 375.52

**Common errors**

- Comparing only today's prices of two bond ladders, ignoring that one provides nominal and the other real cash flows, which are not the same thing.

## Exercises Question 3 (id: Q3)

The I bond composite rate is $f + 2i + f \times i$, where $f$ is the fixed rate and $i$ the semiannual inflation rate. In November 2026: $f = 1.40\%$, $i = 2.04\%$.
(a) Compute the composite rate.
(b) A household has 50,000 dollars that may go toward a home down payment in 3 to 5 years. A friend suggests: "Put it all in I bonds: 5.51% and inflation protection, nothing beats it." Evaluate this suggestion. What limits and alternatives should be considered?

**Reference answer**

(a) $1.40\% + 2 \times 2.04\% + 1.40\% \times 2.04\% \approx 1.40\% + 4.08\% + 0.03\% \approx 5.51\%$.
(b) The suggestion has merit, but not "all of it". First, the purchase limit: at most 10,000 dollars per person per year, so a couple can buy at most 20,000 a year, and 50,000 cannot all go in at once. Second, about 4.08% of the 5.51% is the current inflation part, reset every six months from the CPI; if inflation falls, the composite rate falls. The true real return is set by the 1.40% fixed rate, below TIPS' real yield of about 2.3%. Third, redeeming within 5 years forfeits the last 3 months of interest, and nothing can be redeemed in the first year. For money needed for a down payment in 3 to 5 years, I bonds' strengths are that their nominal value never falls and interest is tax-deferred and state-tax exempt, so part of it can go there; the rest could go to maturity-matched Treasury bills or TIPS (held to maturity, Lesson 3.6, "Credit Risk" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-6-credit-risk/), high-yield savings or money market funds. A down payment is usually tied to home prices, which need not track the CPI, so some slack is also wise.

**Grading points**

- (a) OK: about 5.51%.
- (b) OK: names at least two of the purchase limit, the changing inflation part of the composite rate, the real return being set by the fixed rate, and holding restrictions; gives at least one alternative or combination. Agreeing to put it all in I bonds needs revision.

Numeric answers: comp = 5.51

**Common errors**

- Comparing an I bond's composite (nominal) rate with a TIPS real yield; ignoring that the I bond's fixed rate is what should be compared with the TIPS real yield.

## Exercises Question 4 (id: Q4)

A household holds 300,000 dollars of intermediate and long nominal Treasuries (modified duration 7) and owes a 400,000 dollar 30-year fixed-rate mortgage whose modified duration, valued at market rates, is about 8. Suppose unexpected inflation raises rates at all maturities by 2 percentage points.
(a) Using the duration approximation (Lesson 3.4, "Interest Rate Risk" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-4-interest-rate-risk/), roughly how much does the bonds' market value change? How much does the market value of the mortgage liability change? How much does the household's net worth change (thousand dollars)?
(b) They say: "Inflation is very bad for us, because our bonds will drop sharply." Evaluate this statement. What does this calculation leave out?

**Reference answer**

(a) Bonds: $-7 \times 2\% \times 300 = -42$. The mortgage liability's market value: $-8 \times 2\% \times 400 = -64$, so the liability falls by 64. Net worth rises by about $-42 + 64 = 22$ (thousand dollars).
(b) The statement looks only at the asset side. On the household balance sheet, a fixed-rate mortgage is a nominal liability, like a short position in nominal bonds; when inflation pushes rates up its market value falls, which helps the household, in this example by more than the bond loss. So this household's net exposure to unexpected inflation is actually positive. The calculation leaves out: the mortgage gain cannot be turned into cash at once, showing up instead as a lighter real burden of monthly payments over decades, while a bond loss is realized if the bonds must be sold; the mortgage carries a prepayment option, refinancing when rates fall and holding when they rise, an asymmetry that is an option for the borrower (Lesson 5.2, "Option Basics" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/5-2-options-basics/) not captured by the duration approximation; how the household's other assets (stocks, the house) and income respond to inflation; and the direct effect of higher inflation on living costs.

**Grading points**

- (a) OK: bonds about −42, mortgage liability down about 64, net worth up about 22 (thousand dollars).
- (b) OK: says both assets and liabilities must be considered, a fixed-rate mortgage helps the borrower under inflation, and the net exposure may be positive; mentions at least one omitted factor. Agreeing inflation is very bad needs revision.

Numeric answers: bl = -42, ml = 64, net = 22

**Common errors**

- Looking only at how inflation affects assets, ignoring that the real value of fixed-rate liabilities also falls with inflation.
